lessonTitle: Protozoa and Helminths: Malaria, Worm Classes and Diagnosis

blocks.text: A 31-year-old engineer returns from a three-week posting in West Africa and, ten days later, develops rigors, drenching sweats and a high temperature. The first thick blood film is read as negative, yet a second film the next morning shows ring-shaped parasites inside red cells. Why can a parasite infect in one organ and fever in another, and why does diagnosis depend on repeating the right test?

blocks.markdown: Medical parasitology covers **protozoa** (single-celled eukaryotes, such as *Plasmodium*) and **helminths** (multicellular worms). Malaria remains one of the most important infectious diseases worldwide. It is caused by *Plasmodium* species transmitted by the bite of an infected female *Anopheles* mosquito.

**The Plasmodium life cycle.** (1) An infected mosquito injects **sporozoites** into the skin and they reach the liver within minutes. (2) In the **liver** they invade hepatocytes and multiply (pre-erythrocytic or exo-erythrocytic schizogony); this stage causes no symptoms. In *P. vivax* and *P. ovale* some parasites remain dormant as **hypnozoites** and can cause relapse months later. (3) Hepatocytes rupture and release **merozoites** into the blood. (4) Merozoites invade **red blood cells**, develop into ring-form trophozoites and then **schizonts**, which divide to form new merozoites. (5) The infected red cell **ruptures**, releasing merozoites, parasite products (including haemozoin pigment) and inflammatory mediators. (6) Some parasites become **gametocytes**, which are taken up by a mosquito, where sexual reproduction occurs.

blocks.title: Origin of malarial fever
blocks.text: Fever is caused by the release of merozoites, haemozoin and parasite-derived material when infected red cells rupture. These products stimulate macrophages to release pyrogenic cytokines such as tumour necrosis factor-alpha and interleukin-1. When parasite development is synchronised, rupture occurs together and produces periodic paroxysms of chills, fever and sweating.

blocks.caption: Malaria species and key features
rows: Most severe; infected cells stick to vessel walls (sequestration); cerebral malaria, severe anaemia
Can persist for years at low levels

blocks.title: Linking cycle to fever
blocks.prompt: A patient with P. vivax infection has a first paroxysm on a Monday at midday. When would the next paroxysm be expected, and why?

steps.text: The P. vivax erythrocytic cycle takes about 48 hours, and synchronous rupture of infected red cells releases pyrogens.
The next rupture, and so the next fever, is expected 48 hours later, on Wednesday at midday.

blocks.answer: Wednesday around midday: a tertian pattern from synchronous 48-hour schizont rupture.

blocks.markdown: **Helminths** are classified by shape. **Nematodes** (roundworms) are cylindrical and unsegmented, with a complete gut, for example *Ascaris lumbricoides*, hookworms (*Ancylostoma*, *Necator*), *Strongyloides stercoralis* and *Enterobius vermicularis* (pinworm). **Cestodes** (tapeworms) are flat, ribbon-like, segmented (proglottids) and have a head (scolex) with suckers or hooks but no gut, for example *Taenia saginata* and *Taenia solium*. **Trematodes** (flukes) are flat, leaf-shaped and unsegmented, for example *Schistosoma* species (blood flukes) and liver flukes.

blocks.caption: Classes of helminths
rows: Cylindrical, unsegmented roundworms with complete gut
Flat, segmented tapeworms with scolex; no gut

blocks.markdown: **Choosing the diagnostic test.** In malaria the parasite lives **inside red blood cells**, so the test is on **blood**: thin and thick **Giemsa-stained blood films** examined microscopically (thick film is more sensitive for detection, thin film allows species identification and calculation of **parasitaemia**, the percentage of red cells infected), and rapid antigen tests that detect parasite proteins. A single negative film does not exclude malaria; repeat films are taken at intervals, as in the hook. In intestinal helminthiasis the adult worms live in the gut and shed **eggs, larvae or segments in stool**, so the test is **stool microscopy**, with concentration methods and quantitative egg counts (eggs per gram of stool). Particular situations need a particular specimen: a **sellotape perianal swab** for pinworm eggs, **urine** for *Schistosoma haematobium* eggs, and blood film for *Plasmodium*. Eosinophilia in the blood often hints at tissue-invading helminths.

blocks.title: Calculating parasitaemia
blocks.prompt: On a thin blood film, 30 infected red cells are found among 1 500 red cells counted. What is the parasitaemia?

items: Plasmodium: liver then red cell cycle; rupture releases pyrogens; hypnozoites in vivax and ovale.
Test: blood film for malaria; stool microscopy for most intestinal worms.

blocks.title: The specimen follows the parasite's location
blocks.text: Parasites in blood need blood tests; those in the gut shed eggs into stool. Matching the specimen to the life cycle is the key diagnostic reasoning.

blocks.title: Do not rely on one negative film
blocks.text: In suspected malaria a single negative film does not exclude infection; repeat films are needed. P. falciparum malaria can deteriorate fast and is a medical emergency.

points: Malaria: sporozoites go to the liver, then merozoites invade red cells; rupture releases pyrogens causing fever, periodic when synchronised.
Helminth classes: nematodes (round), cestodes (flat, segmented), trematodes (flat flukes).
Malaria is diagnosed from blood films or rapid tests; intestinal helminths from eggs or larvae in stool.

questions.stem: Which stage of Plasmodium is injected into the skin by the Anopheles mosquito?

distractorRationale.b: Merozoites are released from the liver or from ruptured red cells.
distractorRationale.c: Gametocytes are taken up by the mosquito from blood.
distractorRationale.d: Hypnozoites are dormant liver stages of vivax and ovale.

questions.explanation: Sporozoites in the salivary glands of the mosquito are injected during the blood meal and travel to the liver. The other stages occur later in the cycle.

questions.stem: What is the direct cause of the paroxysms of fever in malaria?

options.text: Rupture of infected red cells releasing merozoites, haemozoin and pyrogenic mediators
Release of lipopolysaccharide from the parasite

questions.correctOptionText: Rupture of infected red cells releasing merozoites, haemozoin and pyrogenic mediators

distractorRationale.d: Plasmodium is a protozoan and has no LPS.

questions.explanation: Synchronous rupture of infected red cells releases parasite products that trigger cytokine release from macrophages, causing chills and fever. The liver stage causes no symptoms.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman treated for Plasmodium vivax malaria returns nine months later with a fresh episode of fever and no new travel. What explains this?

options.text: Reinfection from gametocytes in her blood
Persistence of sporozoites in the skin
A new bacterial co-infection by Anopheles

distractorRationale.b: Gametocytes infect mosquitoes, not the human directly.
distractorRationale.c: Sporozoites reach the liver within minutes.
distractorRationale.d: Mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium, not a bacterial co-infection in this scenario.

questions.explanation: P. vivax and P. ovale form hypnozoites in hepatocytes that can reactivate after months. This is why relapse can occur without new exposure.

questions.stem: A worm recovered from a stool sample is flat, ribbon-like and segmented, with a head bearing suckers. Which class is it?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: tapeworms are segmented with a scolex.

questions.explanation: Cestodes are flat segmented tapeworms with a scolex and no gut. Nematodes are round, and trematodes are leaf-shaped flukes.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old returning traveller has fever and chills. Which investigation is the correct first test for suspected malaria, and which for a patient with chronic diarrhoea and suspected intestinal roundworm?

options.text: Blood films (repeated if negative) for malaria; stool microscopy for eggs for the roundworm
Stool microscopy for malaria; blood films for the roundworm
Urine culture for malaria; sputum Gram stain for the roundworm
Blood films for both, because both are blood parasites

questions.correctOptionText: Blood films (repeated if negative) for malaria; stool microscopy for eggs for the roundworm

distractorRationale.c: Neither parasite is diagnosed by these tests.
distractorRationale.d: Intestinal roundworms are not blood parasites.

questions.explanation: Plasmodium lives in red cells, so blood films detect it; intestinal nematodes shed eggs in stool. The specimen is chosen according to where the parasite or its products are found.

questions.stem: On a thin blood film from a febrile traveller, 45 of 1 800 red cells examined contain ring-form Plasmodium parasites. Calculate the parasitaemia as a percentage of red cells infected.
questions.explanation: Parasitaemia = 45 / 1800 x 100 = 2.5%. This figure is used to gauge severity and to monitor the response to treatment.

questions.stem: A stool preparation contains 24 mg of faeces and 18 Ascaris eggs are counted. Calculate the faecal egg count in eggs per gram of stool (1 g = 1 000 mg).
questions.explanation: 24 mg is 0.024 g, so eggs per gram = 18 / 0.024 = 750. Quantitative egg counts estimate worm burden and are used to monitor treatment.

questions.stem: Describe the life cycle of Plasmodium in the human host and explain how it gives rise to the periodic fever of malaria.
markingGuide: Sporozoites injected by female Anopheles travel to the liver
Multiplication in hepatocytes (asymptomatic); hypnozoites in vivax and ovale
Merozoites released, invade red cells, form rings, trophozoites and schizonts
Schizont rupture releases merozoites, haemozoin and pyrogens that induce cytokine release
Synchronous rupture every 48 h (or 72 h in P. malariae) gives periodic fever; gametocytes taken up by mosquitoes
questions.explanation: The key link is rupture of infected red cells, which releases pyrogenic material. Synchrony of the cycle produces the regular paroxysms.

questions.stem: Distinguish nematodes, cestodes and trematodes by morphology and give one example of each.
markingGuide: Nematodes: cylindrical, unsegmented roundworms with a gut; example Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides or Enterobius
Cestodes: flat, segmented tapeworms with scolex, no gut; example Taenia
Trematodes: flat, leaf-shaped, unsegmented flukes; example Schistosoma or liver fluke
Shape differences are the basis of classification
questions.explanation: Classification by shape and segmentation helps recognition. It also links to different life cycles, specimens and treatments.

questions.stem: Explain why the choice of diagnostic test differs between malaria and intestinal helminthiasis, and how a Plasmodium falciparum infection can still be missed on a single blood film.
markingGuide: Plasmodium lives in red blood cells so diagnosis uses blood: thick and thin Giemsa films and rapid antigen tests
Intestinal worms live in the gut and shed eggs, larvae or segments in stool, so stool microscopy is used
Specific specimens for particular worms (perianal sellotape swab for Enterobius, urine for Schistosoma haematobium)
A single negative film may miss low parasitaemia or sequestered parasites; repeat films at intervals
Rapid antigen tests complement but do not replace microscopy
questions.explanation: The specimen is matched to the stage that circulates or is excreted. Repeated sampling is needed because parasitaemia can be low and fluctuates.
